_spec.purpose: A standalone web edition of the archived visual story.
_spec.law: Facts resolve to the original verified claim record. A layout rebuild does not reverify reporting.

dek.text: UT Arlington is designing an AI trap meant to keep wild screwworm flies and free the sterile ones. The trap isn't built yet. A prototype is expected next spring.

introduction.text: [UT Arlington is coordinating a {{money:c1}} million project funded by the U.S. Department of Agriculture to stop the spread of New World screwworm. The parasite threatens livestock across Texas and other states](c1). [The parasite was declared eliminated from the United States in {{number:c2}} and has reemerged. More than {{number:c2:1}} confirmed animal cases were reported as of November 12th, most of them in Texas, according to the USDA case dashboard UT Arlington cites](c2).

[Female screwworm flies lay eggs in open wounds, and untreated infestations can be fatal](c3). [The center of the project is an AI powered smart trap meant to tell wild flies from sterile ones and females from males](c4).

paragraphs.text: [Today's screwworm traps capture insects indiscriminately and need extensive sorting by hand, which delays confirming the parasite is present](c7). [They can also interfere with the federal program that releases sterile flies to suppress wild populations, because they can't tell sterile flies from wild ones](c8). [USDA has monitored more than {{number:c24:1}} screwworm specific traps since July 2025](c24).

[The planned trap is designed to keep wild flies, especially the females, and release sterile flies and other insects back into the environment](c9). [Wild females are the target because they produce the larvae](c5). [Each detection could feed alerts, location tracking and risk maps to USDA's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service](c10), [and producers and veterinarians would report cases with smartphone photos](c14).

sections.heading: The machine already in the air

paragraphs.text: [An APHIS page says the {{money:c22}} million facility at Moore Air Force Base in Edinburg deploys more than {{number:c22:1}} million sterile flies a week over Texas and Mexico](c22). [USDA developed a strain that yields only male flies for those releases](c23). [Its research service says AI models already help choose where, when and how many sterile flies to release](c17), [work led from its Knipling-Bushland laboratory in Kerrville](c19). [The service also says those models can't predict every scenario](c20).

[The smart trap is still in development. It builds on fruit fly trap research by UT Arlington associate professor Shouyi Wang. Wang expects a prototype by next spring](c6). [The project runs through June {{number:c12}}. Fieldwork takes place in Texas, other states and affected regions of Mexico](c12). [It is one of {{number:c11}} projects selected nationwide in roughly {{money:c11}} million of USDA funding](c11).
[By the end of the project, UT Arlington aims to deliver a field tested system to APHIS](c15). No accuracy figure, field result or catch count exists yet. No trap has been built to produce one.
